investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What does 'anechoic' mean on ultrasound and what causes it?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Anechoic = completely black (no internal echoes), indicating simple fluid — e.g. a simple cyst, the full bladder, or ascites. Typically shows posterior acoustic enhancement behind it.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: Contrast acoustic shadowing with posterior acoustic enhancement.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Acoustic shadowing = dark band BEHIND a strongly reflective/attenuating structure (gallstone, calcification, gas). Posterior acoustic enhancement = bright band BEHIND a fluid-filled structure (cyst), because fluid barely attenuates sound.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: List the key advantages of abdominal ultrasound over CT.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: No ionising radiation (safe, repeatable, good in pregnancy/children), cheap, portable/bedside, real-time and dynamic, and enables image-guided procedures (drains, biopsies).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What are the main limitations of abdominal ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Highly operator-dependent; degraded by bowel gas and body habitus (obesity); poor for the retroperitoneum and pancreas (CT superior); small field of view.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: Which organs/structures does a standard general abdominal US assess, and why fast the patient?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Liver, gallbladder and biliary tree, pancreas (often gas-obscured), spleen, kidneys, aorta, and free fluid. Fasting distends the gallbladder, making stones and wall pathology easier to see.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is the first-line imaging investigation for abnormal LFTs, hepatomegaly, RUQ pain, and HCC surveillance?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Liver ultrasound — cheap, quick, radiation-free; distinguishes diffuse from focal disease and cystic from solid, though it often cannot definitively characterise a solid lesion (needs CT/MRI).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: Describe the ultrasound appearance of fatty liver (hepatic steatosis / NAFLD).
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: A bright/hyperechoic "bright liver" (brighter than the adjacent renal cortex) with posterior beam attenuation and loss of clarity of the intrahepatic vessels and diaphragm.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: List the ultrasound features of cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Cirrhosis: coarse echotexture, nodular surface, small shrunken liver (or hypertrophied caudate/left lobe). Portal hypertension: splenomegaly, ascites, dilated portal vein, recanalised umbilical vein.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: How do a simple cyst and a haemangioma appear on liver ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Simple cyst: anechoic, thin wall, posterior acoustic enhancement (benign). Haemangioma: well-defined, uniformly hyperechoic — the commonest benign solid liver lesion.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is the HCC surveillance protocol in cirrhosis, and what does a new solid nodule mean?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: 6-monthly liver ultrasound (± AFP). A new solid nodule is possible HCC until proven otherwise → refer for contrast-enhanced CT/MRI characterisation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is the first-line, gold-standard investigation for suspected gallstones and gallbladder disease?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Transabdominal ultrasound — cheap, radiation-free and highly sensitive for stones. Used to assess for stones, inflammation (cholecystitis) and biliary obstruction (CBD calibre).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: Give the three classic ultrasound features of a gallstone.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: 1) A mobile, hyperechoic (bright) focus in the gallbladder lumen; 2) posterior acoustic shadowing behind it; 3) movement with gravity/position (rolls to the dependent part). Mobility and shadowing distinguish it from a polyp.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: List the ultrasound features of acute cholecystitis.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), pericholecystic fluid, gallbladder distension, a stone impacted in the neck/cystic duct, and a positive sonographic Murphy's sign (maximal tenderness under the probe over the gallbladder).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: A dilated common bile duct (>6–7 mm) on ultrasound suggests what, and what is the next step if a duct stone is suspected?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: It suggests biliary obstruction — choledocholithiasis (CBD stone), stricture or tumour. Ultrasound is insensitive for CBD stones themselves (bowel gas obscures the distal duct), so proceed to MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound (EUS).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is Charcot's triad and what condition does it indicate?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Fever, RUQ pain and jaundice — indicating ascending cholangitis, a biliary emergency requiring IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage (ERCP). Adding hypotension and confusion gives Reynolds' pentad (septic shock).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: Why is transabdominal ultrasound of the pancreas limited, and what is the main cross-sectional test instead?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: The pancreas is retroperitoneal and frequently obscured by overlying bowel gas, so US visualisation (especially of the tail) is poor. CT is the main cross-sectional test for pancreatic disease.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: In acute pancreatitis, what is the chief role of ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: To look for a gallstone aetiology (gallstones + dilated CBD → gallstone pancreatitis, the commonest cause alongside alcohol) rather than to assess the gland itself. Diagnosis is clinical + amylase/lipase, not imaging.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is a pancreatic pseudocyst on ultrasound and when does it appear?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: A well-defined anechoic (fluid) collection, usually developing more than 4 weeks after an episode of acute pancreatitis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What are the ultrasound features of chronic pancreatitis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: An atrophic gland, calcifications seen as echogenic foci with acoustic shadowing, and a dilated pancreatic duct.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is the 'double-duct sign' and what does it suggest?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Simultaneous dilatation of the common bile duct and pancreatic duct, typically from a hypoechoic mass in the pancreatic head — suggesting pancreatic adenocarcinoma. EUS and CT are superior for detection, staging and biopsy.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is the normal upper limit of splenic length on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Approximately 12–13 cm bipolar (cranio-caudal) length; above this indicates splenomegaly.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: List five broad categories of causes of splenomegaly.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Portal hypertension; haematological malignancy (lymphoma/leukaemia); infection (EBV/infectious mononucleosis, malaria); haemolytic anaemias; and infiltrative disorders (amyloid, sarcoid, storage diseases).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is the role of ultrasound (FAST) in blunt splenic trauma, and what determines management?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: FAST detects free intraperitoneal fluid (haemoperitoneum) and may show laceration/subcapsular haematoma. A haemodynamically UNSTABLE patient goes straight to theatre; a STABLE patient has CT as the definitive test to grade injury and guide conservative management.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: Describe the classic ultrasound appearance of a splenic infarct and two associated conditions.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: A wedge-shaped, peripheral, hypoechoic lesion with its base at the capsule. Associations: septic emboli in infective endocarditis, and sickle cell disease.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: Why are patients with infectious mononucleosis advised to avoid contact sports?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: EBV causes an enlarged, fragile spleen at risk of atraumatic or minor-trauma rupture; contact sports are avoided (around 3–4 weeks / until recovery).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What is the single most important question a renal ultrasound answers in acute kidney injury?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Is there obstruction (hydronephrosis)? Post-renal AKI is reversible if the collecting system is decompressed early, so US screens for a treatable cause before assuming pre-renal or intrinsic disease.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: How does hydronephrosis appear on ultrasound, and which pattern indicates obstructive AKI needing decompression?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Anechoic (black) branching fluid dilating the central renal sinus/pelvicalyceal system. Bilateral hydronephrosis — or unilateral in a single functioning kidney — with rising creatinine indicates post-renal AKI requiring nephrostomy or ureteric stent.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What are the ultrasound features of a renal stone, and why is CT KUB often preferred?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: A bright echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing. US detects renal-pelvis stones and hydronephrosis well, but CT KUB is more sensitive — especially for ureteric stones, which US frequently misses.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: List the ultrasound criteria for a simple (Bosniak I) renal cyst.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Anechoic contents, a thin imperceptible wall, and posterior acoustic enhancement (increased through-transmission). It is benign and needs no follow-up; septa, calcification, wall thickening or solid components make it complex and require CT/MRI.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What ultrasound appearance characterises chronic kidney disease, and what does it imply?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Small, echogenic (bright) kidneys with cortical thinning and loss of corticomedullary differentiation. Bilateral small kidneys imply chronicity and irreversibility, steering away from aggressive investigation of reversible causes.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What aortic diameter defines an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and how is it measured?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Diameter ≥3 cm, measured outer-to-outer in the anteroposterior plane on ultrasound.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: Who does the NHS AAA Screening Programme invite, and what test is used?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Men in the year they turn 65 are offered a one-off abdominal ultrasound scan.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: State the ultrasound surveillance intervals for small and medium AAAs.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Small (3.0–4.4 cm): rescan yearly. Medium (4.5–5.4 cm): rescan 3-monthly.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: List the three triggers for vascular referral / consideration of elective AAA repair.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Diameter ≥5.5 cm, rapid expansion (>1 cm/year), or symptomatic.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: Which imaging is used for a haemodynamically unstable patient with a suspected ruptured AAA?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: None that delays care — they go straight to theatre. Bedside POCUS may rapidly confirm the aneurysm; CT is reserved for stable patients.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: On ultrasound, how does intraperitoneal free fluid appear and where does it collect first?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: It appears anechoic (black) with no wall of its own, tracking around bowel loops. In a supine patient it pools first in the most dependent recesses — Morison's pouch (hepatorenal recess) is the most sensitive single site, along with the splenorenal recess and pelvis/pouch of Douglas.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What ultrasound features distinguish simple from complex ascites, and what does complex fluid suggest?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Simple (transudative) fluid is uniformly anechoic. Complex fluid contains internal echoes, debris, septations or loculation — suggesting exudate, infection (e.g. TB), haemorrhage or malignancy.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: How does the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) classify ascites?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: SAAG = serum albumin − ascitic albumin. SAAG ≥11 g/L indicates portal hypertension (cirrhosis, heart failure — a transudate). SAAG <11 g/L indicates a non-portal/exudative cause (malignancy, infection/TB, pancreatitis, nephrotic syndrome).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: Why is ultrasound-guided paracentesis preferred, and what structures must be avoided?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: US marks a safe fluid pocket clear of hazards, making it safer than a blind tap. Avoid bowel, the bladder, superficial/dilated vessels, and the inferior epigastric arteries running up the rectus sheath. The classic entry is the left iliac fossa.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: How is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) diagnosed and when should you suspect it?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Suspect SBP in any cirrhotic with fever, abdominal pain or unexplained encephalopathy. It is confirmed by an ascitic neutrophil (PMN) count ≥250/mm³ on diagnostic tap, and treated with empirical antibiotics. Any new ascites or decompensating cirrhotic warrants a diagnostic tap to exclude it.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: Why is ultrasound the first-line imaging test for appendicitis in children, young women and pregnancy?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: It avoids ionising radiation. In young women it also assesses gynaecological causes (ovary/adnexa) in the same study.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: List the core positive ultrasound features of acute appendicitis.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Blind-ending, non-compressible, aperistaltic tubular structure from the caecal pole; diameter >6 mm; target sign on cross-section; appendicolith (echogenic + shadowing); periappendiceal fluid/echogenic inflamed fat; wall hyperaemia on Doppler.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What is the critical limitation of ultrasound in suspected appendicitis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: It is operator-dependent, and a non-visualised appendix does NOT exclude appendicitis — US can rule in but cannot rule out.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: If US is negative or equivocal but clinical suspicion of appendicitis persists, what next?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Escalate: CT in adults, MRI in pregnancy, or observation / diagnostic laparoscopy — do not discharge.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What single test is mandatory in any woman of childbearing age with RIF pain, and why?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: A pregnancy test, to exclude ectopic pregnancy before committing to a diagnosis or imaging pathway.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: Why is a full bladder needed for a transabdominal pelvic ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: The distended bladder displaces gas-filled bowel loops out of the pelvis and acts as a fluid acoustic window, transmitting sound to allow the uterus, ovaries and adnexa to be seen.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: Which probe and approach are used for TAUS?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: A low-frequency curvilinear probe applied suprapubically over the lower abdomen.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: List the key structures assessed on transabdominal pelvic ultrasound.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Uterus (size, position, fibroids, endometrial thickness), ovaries and adnexa, free fluid in the pouch of Douglas, and the bladder itself.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: Give two advantages and two limitations of TAUS versus transvaginal scanning.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Advantages: non-invasive, panoramic overview, good for large/extra-pelvic masses, suitable for children and virgins. Limitations: lower resolution, degraded by obesity/bowel gas, useless with an empty bladder, retroverted uterus hard to see.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: In suspected ectopic pregnancy, what does a normal-looking TAUS mean?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: It does not exclude pathology. A technically limited or empty-bladder transabdominal scan is falsely reassuring, so proceed to transvaginal ultrasound.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: How does bladder preparation for transvaginal ultrasound differ from transabdominal, and why?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: TVUS requires an EMPTY bladder (a full bladder pushes organs out of the probe's near field and degrades the close-up image), whereas transabdominal scanning needs a FULL bladder as an acoustic window.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: At what point is an intrauterine gestational sac expected on TVUS, and what does confirming one mean?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: From about 5 weeks / when serum hCG exceeds the discriminatory zone (~1500 IU/L). Confirming an intrauterine pregnancy makes ectopic very unlikely (heterotopic is rare, higher only with IVF).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What endometrial thickness on TVUS is reassuring vs concerning in postmenopausal bleeding, and what is the next step if thickened?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: <4–5 mm is reassuring; a thickened endometrium (≥4–5 mm) requires hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy to exclude endometrial cancer.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: Which TVUS features suggest a tubal ectopic pregnancy?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: An adnexal mass separate from the ovary, an echogenic 'tubal ring', and free fluid in the pouch of Douglas — especially with an empty uterus and positive hCG.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: When is TVUS inappropriate, and what is the alternative?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: When the patient is not sexually active, cannot tolerate a speculum, declines, or in some cultural situations. Use transabdominal ultrasound (full bladder) instead. TVUS always needs consent and a chaperone.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: How is endometrial thickness correctly measured on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Double-layer (both endometrial surfaces) at the widest point on the transvaginal SAGITTAL/midline view, excluding the hypoechoic myometrial halo and any intracavity fluid.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: In a woman with postmenopausal bleeding, what endometrial thickness is reassuring, and what is the cut-off for further investigation?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: ≤4 mm is reassuring (endometrial cancer very unlikely). >4 mm requires hysteroscopy plus endometrial biopsy (pipelle) to exclude endometrial carcinoma.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: How do fibroids and adenomyosis differ on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Fibroid = focal, well-defined rounded hypoechoic myometrial mass (may shadow/calcify/degenerate). Adenomyosis = diffusely enlarged 'globular' uterus, heterogeneous myometrium with cysts and a poorly defined/thickened junctional zone; no discrete mass.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What ultrasound features suggest an endometrial polyp, and what test helps delineate it?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Focal echogenic thickening within the endometrial cavity with a single feeding vessel on Doppler. Saline infusion sonography (sonohysterography) distends the cavity to outline it.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: How do you distinguish a bicornuate from a septate uterus, and why does it matter?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Bicornuate: the EXTERNAL fundal contour is split (fundal cleft/two horns). Septate: external contour is intact/single with an internal septum. The distinction changes management (septum can be resected hysteroscopically).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What three ultrasound features define a simple (benign, usually functional) ovarian cyst?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Anechoic (fluid-filled), thin smooth wall with no septations or solid components, and posterior acoustic enhancement. Usually a follicular or corpus luteal cyst — benign and typically resolves spontaneously.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: How do you distinguish an endometrioma from a dermoid on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Endometrioma ("chocolate cyst") = homogeneous low-level "ground-glass" echoes, no solid vascular nodule. Dermoid/mature teratoma = echogenic focus with fat and calcification and "tip of the iceberg" acoustic shadowing obscuring the deep wall.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What is the current ultrasound threshold for polycystic ovarian morphology, and does it diagnose PCOS?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: ≥20 follicles (2–9 mm) per ovary and/or ovarian volume >10 mL. Ultrasound alone does NOT diagnose PCOS — PCOS requires 2 of 3 Rotterdam criteria (oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic morphology).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What ultrasound features suggest an ovarian malignancy, and what does RMI combine?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Solid components, thick (>3 mm) septations, papillary projections, bilaterality, ascites, and high Doppler flow. RMI = Ultrasound score × Menopausal status × CA-125; RMI >200 prompts gynae-oncology referral.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: Why can ovarian torsion have preserved Doppler flow, and what does this mean clinically?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: The ovary has a dual blood supply (ovarian and uterine arteries), so arterial flow may persist despite torsion. A normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion — clinical suspicion mandates urgent laparoscopy to detorse and salvage the ovary.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: Which ultrasound approach is first-line for early pregnancy assessment, and why?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS). The probe sits closer to the pelvic organs, giving better resolution of early landmarks than transabdominal scanning. It is performed in the Early Pregnancy Assessment Unit (EPAU) alongside serum hCG.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: List the normal early ultrasound landmarks and their approximate gestational ages.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Intrauterine gestational sac ~4.5–5 weeks; yolk sac ~5.5 weeks; fetal pole with heartbeat ~6 weeks. The yolk sac is the first structure confirming a true intrauterine pregnancy.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What is the discriminatory zone and how is it used?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: The serum hCG level (~>1500 IU/L) above which an intrauterine gestational sac should be visible on TVUS. If hCG is above this and the uterus is empty, ectopic pregnancy becomes much more likely.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: State the NICE/RCOG ultrasound criteria for a non-viable (miscarried) pregnancy.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Fetal pole with crown-rump length ≥7 mm and NO heartbeat, OR mean gestational sac diameter ≥25 mm with no fetal pole. If below these thresholds or uncertain, rescan in 7–14 days before diagnosing miscarriage.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What ultrasound features suggest an ectopic pregnancy?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Empty uterus with positive pregnancy test (pregnancy of unknown location), adnexal mass separate from the ovary, tubal 'ring/bagel' sign, free fluid in the pouch of Douglas (haemoperitoneum), and a pseudogestational sac in the uterus. Serial hCG with a suboptimal rise supports the diagnosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What is the ellipsoid formula for estimating bladder volume on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Volume (mL) ≈ height × width × depth × 0.52, using three orthogonal diameters (craniocaudal, transverse and anteroposterior) measured in cm.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What post-void residual (PVR) volume is considered normal, and what is acceptable in the elderly?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Normal PVR is <50 mL; up to ~100 mL is acceptable, particularly in elderly patients. Persistently raised values indicate incomplete emptying.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: Why must a post-void residual be scanned immediately after voiding?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Any delay allows urine to re-accumulate from the kidneys, falsely raising the residual and making emptying look worse than it is.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: How do bladder stones and bladder tumours differ on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Stones are echogenic, mobile (shift with patient position) and cast an acoustic shadow; tumours are non-mobile wall-based soft-tissue masses that do not move.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What complications suggest high-pressure chronic retention, and what must you watch for after catheterisation?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Bilateral hydronephrosis and post-obstructive AKI (rising creatinine). After catheterising, monitor for post-obstructive diuresis and electrolyte shifts.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: In what gestational window is the UK routine dating scan offered?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Between 11+2 and 14+1 weeks of gestation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: Which measurement dates a first-trimester pregnancy most accurately, and over what range?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Crown-rump length (CRL), reliable from roughly 8.5 to 14 weeks. Beyond ~14 weeks (CRL >~84 mm) it becomes unreliable and head circumference is used instead.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What ultrasound sign indicates a dichorionic twin pregnancy, and what indicates a monochorionic one?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Dichorionic = lambda / twin-peak sign (triangular placental wedge between the membranes). Monochorionic = T-sign (membrane meets placenta at 90° with no wedge).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: Why is chorionicity best determined at the dating scan?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Chorionicity is most accurately assessed in the first trimester, and it determines risk: monochorionic (shared placenta) twins are at risk of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome and need increased surveillance.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: When there is a discrepancy between LMP-based dates and scan dates, which is used to set the EDD?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: The scan (CRL) date supersedes LMP-based dating and sets the estimated due date, standardising the timing of later screening.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What is nuchal translucency and when is it measured?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: The ultrasound-measured anechoic fluid space at the back of the fetal neck, measured on a mid-sagittal image as part of the UK first-trimester combined screening test, offered between 11+2 and 14+1 weeks.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What are the three components of the combined test?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Maternal age + nuchal translucency + serum biochemistry (β-hCG and PAPP-A), combined into a single numerical chance of trisomy 21, 18 and 13.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What biochemical pattern is typical of trisomy 21 on first-trimester screening?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Raised β-hCG and low PAPP-A. (NT is also typically increased.)

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What is offered after a higher-chance result (commonly ≥1 in 150)?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: The offer of NIPT (cell-free fetal DNA) as an intermediate non-invasive step, or definitive diagnostic testing: chorionic villus sampling (CVS, ~11–14 wks) or amniocentesis (from ~15 wks). Invasive tests carry ~0.5–1% miscarriage risk.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What is the alternative if the NT/combined test window is missed?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: The second-trimester quadruple test (14–20 weeks), which screens for trisomy 21 only using maternal serum (AFP, hCG, uE3, inhibin A).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: When is the NHS anomaly scan offered, and under which programme?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Between 18+0 and 20+6 weeks of gestation, under the Fetal Anomaly Screening Programme (FASP).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What are the 'lemon' and 'banana' signs and what do they indicate?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Cranial signs of open spina bifida: the 'lemon' sign is scalloping of the frontal skull bones, and the 'banana' sign is the curved cerebellum wrapped around the brainstem with an obliterated cisterna magna.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: How does exomphalos differ from gastroschisis on the anomaly scan?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Exomphalos: herniated abdominal contents covered by a membranous sac at the cord insertion, associated with aneuploidy. Gastroschisis: free-floating uncovered bowel loops, usually to the right of the cord, typically isolated.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What does the scan report about the placenta, and what follow-up may be triggered?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: It documents placental location; a low-lying placenta or suspected placenta praevia is flagged for a repeat scan at around 32–36 weeks.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What is a 'soft marker' and give three examples.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: A minor ultrasound finding that is not an anomaly itself but may prompt reassessment of aneuploidy risk. Examples: echogenic bowel, echogenic intracardiac focus, mild pyelectasis, choroid plexus cyst.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: Which single biometry measurement is most sensitive for detecting fetal growth restriction?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Abdominal circumference (AC) — it reflects fetal liver glycogen and subcutaneous fat, so it falls early in placental insufficiency (asymmetric, head-sparing FGR).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: How is fetal growth restriction (FGR) defined on a growth scan?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: EFW or AC below the 10th centile, especially with a static or falling trajectory across serial scans. Placental insufficiency typically produces an asymmetric pattern (low AC, preserved HC).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What two non-biometry parameters are assessed alongside size to judge fetal wellbeing?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Liquor volume (amniotic fluid index / deepest pool — oligohydramnios suggests placental insufficiency) and umbilical artery Doppler (raised resistance / absent or reversed end-diastolic flow indicates placental compromise).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What defines macrosomia / large-for-gestational-age, and what is the main association and intrapartum risk?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: EFW above the 90th centile. Associated with maternal diabetes; the key intrapartum risk is shoulder dystocia.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: Name three clinical indications for arranging a growth scan.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Any of: SFH small/large for dates or crossing centiles, reduced fetal movements, and maternal risk factors — hypertension/pre-eclampsia, diabetes, previous SGA baby or stillbirth, multiple pregnancy.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What is the progressive umbilical artery Doppler sequence in worsening placental insufficiency?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Raised pulsatility index (PI) → absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) → reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF). REDF is the most advanced arterial sign and indicates severe insufficiency with high stillbirth risk.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What does a falling MCA pulsatility index indicate, and what is the cerebroplacental ratio?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: A falling MCA PI reflects cerebral vasodilation — the brain-sparing effect of a hypoxic fetus redistributing blood to the brain. CPR = MCA PI ÷ UA PI; a low CPR flags redistribution and predicts adverse outcome.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: Why is MCA peak systolic velocity (PSV) measured, and what threshold triggers action?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Raised MCA PSV detects fetal anaemia (e.g. rhesus/red-cell alloimmunisation, parvovirus B19) due to low viscosity and a high-output state. PSV >1.5 multiples of the median (MoM) is the trigger to arrange intrauterine transfusion.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What ductus venosus finding is a late, pre-terminal sign, and how is it used?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: An absent or reversed a-wave reflects myocardial decompensation and raised right atrial pressure. It is a late sign used to time delivery in very preterm fetal growth restriction.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What uterine artery Doppler pattern predicts pre-eclampsia and FGR?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Persistently high resistance with early diastolic "notching" reflects failed trophoblastic invasion of the spiral arteries and predicts pre-eclampsia and fetal growth restriction.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What are the five components of the biophysical profile and the maximum score?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Fetal breathing movements, gross body movements, fetal tone, amniotic fluid volume, and a reactive CTG (non-stress test). Each scored 2 or 0, maximum 10.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: How is a BPP score interpreted?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: 8–10 = reassuring/normal; 6 = equivocal (repeat or deliver depending on gestation); ≤4 = abnormal, strong evidence of fetal hypoxia, usually prompts delivery.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What defines a normal amniotic fluid component on BPP?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: A single deepest vertical pool of ≥2 cm. Less than 2 cm (oligohydramnios) reflects chronic placental insufficiency.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: Which biophysical activities are lost first and last in progressive fetal hypoxia?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: CTG reactivity and fetal breathing movements are lost first (most hypoxia-sensitive); fetal tone is lost last (most resistant), reflecting CNS centres of differing sensitivity.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What is the modified biophysical profile?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: A shorter screening test using only two components: amniotic fluid volume plus a CTG (non-stress test).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What is the first-line imaging test for suspected DVT?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Compression ultrasound (CUS) with Doppler — cheap, portable, radiation-free, directly interrogating the proximal deep veins (common femoral, femoral, popliteal).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What is the single most important ultrasound sign of DVT?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Non-compressibility — a normal vein collapses completely under gentle probe pressure, whereas a vein containing thrombus does not compress.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Define proximal versus distal DVT.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Proximal (above-knee) = popliteal and femoral veins. Distal = calf veins. Proximal DVT carries the higher risk of PE.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: In the UK pathway, what does a two-level Wells score of ≥2 ("DVT likely") trigger?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Proximal leg vein ultrasound within 4 hours; if not available, give interim anticoagulation plus a D-dimer and scan within 24 hours.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What does a negative proximal US with a positive D-dimer prompt?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: A repeat proximal ultrasound in about 6–8 days, to catch a calf-vein thrombus that may have propagated proximally.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What is the primary spectral Doppler parameter used to grade internal carotid artery stenosis, and which way does it move?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Peak systolic velocity (PSV) in the ICA — velocity rises as the lumen narrows, so a higher PSV indicates a tighter stenosis. Supported by ICA/CCA PSV ratio and end-diastolic velocity (EDV).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Which patients with carotid stenosis should be referred for carotid endarterectomy, and in what timeframe?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Symptomatic patients (recent TIA or non-disabling ischaemic stroke in the anterior circulation) with 50–99% NASCET stenosis — ideally operated within 2 weeks of symptom onset.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: How is degree of carotid stenosis reported, and what is the main clinical threshold?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: As a percentage using NASCET criteria. ~PSV ≥125 cm/s corresponds to ≥50% stenosis — the threshold for considering surgery in symptomatic patients (≥70% carries the greatest benefit).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Which carotid Doppler findings are generally NOT treated with endarterectomy?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Near-occlusion / string sign, 100% (complete) occlusion, and asymptomatic stenosis — all managed medically with antiplatelet, statin, BP control and smoking cessation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What plaque features on B-mode matter, and which is highest risk for embolism?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Calcified plaque is bright with acoustic shadowing; soft/echolucent plaque is dark and carries the highest embolic risk; ulcerated plaque has a surface crater. Also assess intima-media thickness.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What is the normal spectral Doppler waveform of a healthy peripheral limb artery, and what are its three components?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Triphasic: (1) sharp systolic forward-flow upstroke, (2) brief early-diastolic flow reversal below baseline (elastic recoil against high peripheral resistance), (3) small late-diastolic forward flow.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: How does the arterial waveform change distal to a significant stenosis or occlusion?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: It progressively damps: triphasic → biphasic (loss of reversal) → monophasic (low-velocity, rounded, continuous forward flow with slow upstroke). A monophasic damped signal means significant disease lies proximal to the probe.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What peak systolic velocity ratio across a stenosis indicates a haemodynamically significant (≥50%) narrowing?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: A velocity ratio >2:1 (PSV within the stenosis compared to the normal segment just proximal) indicates ≥50% diameter stenosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Give the ABPI value bands and their interpretation.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: 0.9–1.2 normal; 0.5–0.9 intermittent claudication; <0.5 critical limb ischaemia; >1.3 falsely elevated due to incompressible calcified vessels (diabetes, CKD).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What are the 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia and why do they matter?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paraesthesia, Perishingly cold, Paralysis. It is a surgical emergency threatening the limb within hours — needs urgent revascularisation/embolectomy and heparin; do NOT delay for elaborate imaging.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What is renal artery Doppler used to screen for, and what is its role?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: It is the non-invasive first-line screening test for renal artery stenosis (RAS), assessing renal artery velocities, intrarenal waveforms, kidney size and resistive index. Anatomical confirmation is by CT or MR angiography.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: List the key clinical indications for renal artery Doppler.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Resistant/refractory hypertension; hypertension in a young person (FMD) or with an epigastric/flank bruit; recurrent 'flash' pulmonary oedema; unexplained or asymmetric renal size; and a rise in creatinine after starting an ACEi/ARB (clue to bilateral RAS or RAS in a solitary kidney).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Contrast the two main causes of RAS.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Atherosclerosis — older patients, ostial/proximal lesion, commonest cause. Fibromuscular dysplasia — younger women, mid-to-distal vessel, 'string of beads' on angiography, responds well to angioplasty.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What Doppler findings indicate significant renal artery stenosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Raised peak systolic velocity at the stenosis (e.g. >180–200 cm/s); elevated renal-aortic ratio (>3.5); and a downstream intrarenal 'tardus-parvus' waveform (delayed slow systolic upstroke, low resistive index). Also look for a small kidney.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: How is RAS managed?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Often medical: ACEi/ARB with renal-function monitoring plus cardiovascular risk reduction. Angioplasty ± stent is selective (FMD, flash pulmonary oedema, rapidly declining function); routine stenting of atherosclerotic RAS does not clearly improve outcomes.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What is the normal direction and character of portal vein flow on Doppler?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Hepatopetal (towards the liver), gently phasic, low velocity (~15–40 cm/s). The main portal vein measures up to ~13 mm.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Which single Doppler finding is most specific for portal hypertension, and name three supporting signs.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Reversed (hepatofugal) portal flow. Supporting signs: dilated portal vein >13 mm, splenomegaly, ascites, recanalised umbilical vein, and porto-systemic collaterals/varices.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: How does tumour thrombus differ from bland thrombus in the portal vein on Doppler, and what does it suggest?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Tumour thrombus shows arterial flow WITHIN the thrombus (bland thrombus is avascular). Arterial signal within a portal vein thrombus suggests underlying hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Give the classic Doppler and morphological features of Budd-Chiari syndrome.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Hepatic vein outflow obstruction: absent/reversed/turbulent hepatic vein flow, hepatic vein thrombosis or webs, caudate lobe hypertrophy (spared due to separate IVC drainage), and ascites.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Why is hepatic artery patency critical to check after liver transplant?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Hepatic artery thrombosis is the feared early post-transplant complication. The transplanted biliary tree depends solely on arterial supply, so arterial occlusion threatens the graft with ischaemic biliary necrosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: On pre-operative vein mapping, what minimum vein diameter is generally wanted for a successful AVF?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: A patent, distensible, superficial vein of at least ~2–2.5 mm diameter (measured under a light tourniquet).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: State the 'rule of 6s' for AVF maturation.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: By about 6 weeks: access flow >600 mL/min, vein diameter >6 mm, and vein depth <6 mm from the skin — then it is ready to cannulate.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What is the preferred order of vascular access and of fistula site for haemodialysis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Access: AVF > AV graft > central venous catheter. Fistula: radiocephalic (Brescia–Cimino) first, then brachiocephalic, then brachiobasilic transposition.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Which Doppler findings suggest a haemodynamically significant fistula stenosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Focally raised peak systolic velocity with a PSV ratio >2–3 across the lesion (typically juxta-anastomotic or outflow), plus reduced overall access flow.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What ultrasound/clinical picture indicates dialysis access steal syndrome?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Distal hand ischaemia (pain, pallor, cold, weak pulse) with retrograde arterial flow in the artery distal to the anastomosis — a threatened hand needs urgent vascular review.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A gallbladder ultrasound shows a bright (hyperechoic) focus with a dark band extending deep to it that moves with position. What is this appearance?
options: Anechoic cyst with posterior acoustic enhancement
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: A bright, mobile focus casting an acoustic shadow (dark band behind it) is the classic appearance of a gallstone. Shadowing occurs because the stone strongly reflects/absorbs sound so little passes deep to it.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: Which of the following is a recognised LIMITATION of abdominal ultrasound?
options: It is highly operator-dependent and limited by bowel gas
It cannot be performed at the bedside
It provides an excellent view of the retroperitoneal pancreas
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: It is highly operator-dependent and limited by bowel gas
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: US is operator-dependent and easily obscured by bowel gas and obesity, and is poor for the retroperitoneum/pancreas. It uses NO ionising radiation, is safe in pregnancy, and can be done at the bedside — those are advantages, not limitations.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A structure appears completely black (anechoic) with increased brightness in the tissues immediately behind it. This is most consistent with:
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: Anechoic (black) content with posterior acoustic enhancement (brightening deep to it) indicates a simple fluid-filled structure such as a cyst. Calcification and gas cause shadowing, not enhancement; fibrosis and fat are echogenic, not anechoic.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A 55-year-old with type 2 diabetes has mildly deranged LFTs. Ultrasound shows a liver that is diffusely brighter than the right kidney, with poor visualisation of the deep hepatic vessels and diaphragm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: A diffusely bright/hyperechoic liver with posterior beam attenuation and loss of vessel and diaphragm clarity is the classic "bright liver" of steatosis/NAFLD, strongly associated with type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A patient with known alcohol-related cirrhosis attends for routine 6-monthly surveillance ultrasound. A new 2 cm solid nodule is identified that was not present previously. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and repeat ultrasound in 5 years
Arrange contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the liver
No action as this is a simple cyst
Commence oral antibiotics for a liver abscess
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: Arrange contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the liver
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: A new focal solid lesion in a cirrhotic liver is hepatocellular carcinoma until proven otherwise. Ultrasound detects it but cannot characterise it, so multiphase contrast-enhanced CT or MRI is required.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: Which ultrasound appearance is most characteristic of a simple hepatic cyst?
options: Anechoic lesion with a thin wall and posterior acoustic enhancement
Coarse nodular parenchyma with a shrunken outline
Bright liver with posterior beam attenuation
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: Anechoic lesion with a thin wall and posterior acoustic enhancement
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: A simple cyst is anechoic (fluid-filled, black) with an imperceptibly thin wall and posterior acoustic enhancement. The uniformly hyperechoic lesion describes a haemangioma, and the "target" lesion describes a metastasis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A 45-year-old woman with colicky RUQ pain has an ultrasound showing a bright, echogenic focus in the gallbladder lumen that casts a dark band beneath it and rolls to the dependent side when she is repositioned. What is the single most specific feature confirming this is a gallstone?
options: Posterior acoustic shadowing with mobility on repositioning
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: Posterior acoustic shadowing with mobility on repositioning
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: Brightness alone can be seen with polyps or sludge. The combination of posterior acoustic shadowing (the stone reflects/absorbs the beam) plus mobility with gravity is what reliably identifies a gallstone and distinguishes it from a fixed polyp or non-shadowing sludge.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A 60-year-old man has RUQ pain and fever. Ultrasound shows a distended gallbladder with a 5 mm thick wall, a rim of pericholecystic fluid, a stone lodged in the gallbladder neck, and maximal tenderness as the probe presses over the gallbladder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: Wall thickening >3 mm, pericholecystic fluid, distension, a stone impacted in the neck and a positive sonographic Murphy's sign are the hallmark features of acute cholecystitis. Biliary colic has no inflammatory signs; cholangitis is characterised by jaundice with duct dilatation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A patient presents with fever, RUQ pain and jaundice. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct at 9 mm but no visible duct stone. What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?
options: Reassure and repeat ultrasound in 6 weeks
IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage (ERCP)
Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the next available list
Oral ursodeoxycholic acid to dissolve stones
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage (ERCP)
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: Fever, RUQ pain and jaundice is Charcot's triad — ascending cholangitis, an infected obstructed biliary tree and a medical emergency. It requires prompt IV antibiotics and urgent decompression of the biliary system, typically by ERCP. A non-visualised duct stone does not exclude obstruction, as ultrasound is insensitive for CBD stones.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A 52-year-old man presents with severe epigastric pain and a serum lipase three times the upper limit of normal. He is admitted with acute pancreatitis. What is the chief reason an abdominal ultrasound is requested?
options: To confirm the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis
To assess the pancreas for necrosis
To measure the severity score of pancreatitis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: Diagnosis of acute pancreatitis is clinical plus raised amylase/lipase, not imaging. US is used chiefly to look for gallstones and a dilated CBD (gallstone pancreatitis). CT — not US — assesses necrosis and severity, ideally at 48–72h.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A 60-year-old woman has painless obstructive jaundice and 6 kg of weight loss. Ultrasound shows dilatation of both the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and repeat ultrasound in 6 months
Urgent CT and/or endoscopic ultrasound referral
ERCP alone with no cross-sectional imaging
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: Urgent CT and/or endoscopic ultrasound referral
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: The double-duct sign with painless obstructive jaundice and weight loss strongly suggests pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. US may raise the suspicion, but CT and EUS are far superior for detection, staging and biopsy, so urgent referral is needed.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: An ultrasound of a patient with a long history of alcohol excess shows an atrophic pancreas with echogenic foci that cast acoustic shadows and a dilated pancreatic duct. Which diagnosis do these features best fit?
options: Normal pancreas obscured by bowel gas
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: Atrophy, calcifications (echogenic foci with shadowing) and a dilated pancreatic duct are the classic US features of chronic pancreatitis. An anechoic collection would suggest a pseudocyst, and a focal hypoechoic mass would suggest adenocarcinoma.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A 19-year-old with sore throat, fever and fatigue has a positive monospot test. Ultrasound shows a homogeneously enlarged, soft spleen measuring 15 cm. Which advice is most important?
options: Avoid contact sports until recovery due to rupture risk
Repeat ultrasound daily until the spleen normalises
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: Avoid contact sports until recovery due to rupture risk
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) causes an enlarged, fragile spleen prone to rupture. The key safety advice is to avoid contact sports (typically ~3–4 weeks/until recovery). Splenectomy and anticoagulation are not indicated, and antibiotics do not treat this viral illness.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A 25-year-old is brought in after a road traffic collision with LUQ pain and a heart rate of 130 with systolic BP 80 mmHg. FAST shows free fluid in the splenorenal recess. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: CT abdomen with contrast to grade the injury
Immediate resuscitation and transfer to theatre
MRI abdomen to characterise the spleen
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: Immediate resuscitation and transfer to theatre
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: A positive FAST in a haemodynamically UNSTABLE trauma patient is a surgical emergency. Resuscitate and go to theatre without delay — CT is only appropriate for the haemodynamically stable patient to grade injury and plan conservative management.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: During an abdominal ultrasound, a 2 cm rounded nodule with the same echotexture as the spleen is seen adjacent to the splenic hilum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: A splenunculus is a common normal variant: a small round nodule near the hilum with echotexture identical to the spleen. It should not be mistaken for a mass or lymph node. An infarct is wedge-shaped and hypoechoic, a cyst is anechoic, and an abscess is a complex collection in a septic patient.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A 72-year-old man presents with anuria and a creatinine that has tripled over 48 hours. Renal ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis, a grossly distended bladder and a post-void residual of 900 mL. What is the most likely mechanism of his AKI?
options: Bladder outlet obstruction causing post-renal AKI
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.answer: Bladder outlet obstruction causing post-renal AKI
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: Bilateral hydronephrosis with a chronically distended bladder and a large post-void residual localises the obstruction to the bladder outlet (e.g. prostatic enlargement). This is post-renal AKI; catheterisation relieves the obstruction. Pre-renal and intrinsic causes do not produce hydronephrosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A renal ultrasound performed for flank pain demonstrates a bright echogenic focus in the renal pelvis with clean posterior acoustic shadowing, and mild ipsilateral hydronephrosis. Ureteric colic is suspected but no ureteric stone is seen. What is the best next investigation?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: The echogenic focus with posterior shadowing is a stone. US is insensitive for ureteric stones, so a non-contrast CT KUB is the most sensitive test to confirm a ureteric calculus, locate it and guide management. It also detects the stone burden US cannot visualise along the ureter.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: During an ultrasound for haematuria, a 3 cm heterogeneous solid mass is found arising from the upper pole of the right kidney. It shows no posterior acoustic enhancement. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure — this is a simple cyst
Arrange contrast-enhanced CT for characterisation and staging, and refer to urology
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.answer: Arrange contrast-enhanced CT for characterisation and staging, and refer to urology
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: A solid renal mass is a possible renal cell carcinoma until proven otherwise. The absence of posterior enhancement argues against a simple cyst. Contrast CT characterises and stages the lesion and urology referral is required. Angiomyolipoma (echogenic fat) is a differential but still needs CT to confirm macroscopic fat.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A 66-year-old man attends AAA screening. His abdominal ultrasound shows an infrarenal aortic diameter of 4.8 cm. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Immediate referral for elective open repair
Urgent CT angiography to exclude rupture
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: A medium AAA (4.5–5.4 cm) is placed on 3-monthly ultrasound surveillance. It has not reached the 5.5 cm threshold for elective repair, and the patient is asymptomatic and stable, so CT is not indicated.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A 74-year-old man collapses with sudden severe back pain. He is hypotensive with a pulsatile abdominal mass and a known 6 cm AAA. What is the most appropriate management?
options: CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis before any intervention
Repeat outpatient ultrasound to confirm expansion
Immediate transfer to theatre for emergency repair
Commence antihypertensives and reassess in 24 hours
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.answer: Immediate transfer to theatre for emergency repair
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: The triad of sudden pain, pulsatile mass and hypotension indicates a ruptured AAA. A haemodynamically unstable patient must go straight to theatre — imaging must not delay definitive surgery.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: Which statement about the role of ultrasound in AAA is most accurate?
options: Ultrasound is the definitive test for pre-operative EVAR planning
Ultrasound is radiation-free, cheap and reliably measures maximal aortic diameter
Ultrasound is used to diagnose rupture in unstable patients before theatre
An AAA is defined as an aortic diameter ≥2 cm on ultrasound
Ultrasound cannot detect mural thrombus within the aneurysm sac
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.answer: Ultrasound is radiation-free, cheap and reliably measures maximal aortic diameter
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: These properties make US ideal for screening and surveillance. CT angiography — not US — is used for pre-operative planning and to diagnose rupture in stable patients. An AAA is ≥3 cm, and US does show mural thrombus.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A 58-year-old man with known alcoholic cirrhosis presents with a distended abdomen. Bedside ultrasound is requested to confirm ascites. In a supine patient, which single site is the most sensitive for detecting a small volume of free fluid?
options: The subphrenic space above the spleen
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: In a supine patient, Morison's pouch — the potential space between the liver and right kidney — is the most dependent upper-abdominal recess and the most sensitive location for detecting small volumes of free fluid, which appears as an anechoic stripe. This is also a key window in the FAST scan.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A cirrhotic patient with new ascites undergoes a diagnostic tap. The ascitic fluid appears clear on ultrasound (uniformly anechoic). Serum albumin is 30 g/L and ascitic albumin is 15 g/L. What does this indicate?
options: Serum-ascites albumin gradient of 15 g/L, indicating portal hypertension
Serum-ascites albumin gradient of 15 g/L, indicating a malignant exudate
Serum-ascites albumin gradient of 45 g/L, indicating infection
A low gradient consistent with peritoneal TB
An indeterminate gradient requiring cytology to classify
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.answer: Serum-ascites albumin gradient of 15 g/L, indicating portal hypertension
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: SAAG = 30 − 15 = 15 g/L. A SAAG ≥11 g/L reliably indicates portal hypertension (here from cirrhosis), producing a transudate that is typically uniformly anechoic on ultrasound. A low gradient (<11 g/L) would instead point to exudative causes such as malignancy or infection.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A 62-year-old woman with cirrhosis presents with fever, diffuse abdominal pain and new confusion. Ultrasound confirms a moderate volume of ascites. A diagnostic tap is performed. Which finding confirms the most important diagnosis to exclude?
options: Positive ascitic fluid cytology for malignant cells
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: Fever, abdominal pain and encephalopathy in a cirrhotic strongly suggest spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), a medical emergency. SBP is diagnosed by an ascitic polymorphonuclear (neutrophil) count ≥250/mm³ and requires prompt empirical antibiotics. The other findings relate to classifying the ascites but do not diagnose SBP.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A 9-year-old boy has 24 hours of central pain that has moved to the right iliac fossa, anorexia and a low-grade fever. Diagnosis is uncertain and imaging is requested. Which first-line investigation is most appropriate?
options: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: In children, US is first-line imaging as it avoids ionising radiation. CT would be reserved for equivocal cases where suspicion persists after US.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: Which ultrasound finding is most specific for acute appendicitis?
options: A compressible tubular structure measuring 4 mm
Free fluid in the pouch of Douglas alone
A blind-ending, non-compressible tube from the caecal pole measuring >6 mm
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.answer: A blind-ending, non-compressible tube from the caecal pole measuring >6 mm
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: The diagnostic combination is a blind-ending, non-compressible, aperistaltic tube >6 mm. A compressible 4 mm structure is normal, and a non-visualised appendix does not confirm or exclude the diagnosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A 26-year-old woman with RIF pain has an ultrasound that fails to visualise the appendix, but her pain and localised peritonism persist. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the same ultrasound in one week
Escalate to CT or proceed to observation / diagnostic laparoscopy
Immediately start long-term oral antibiotics at home
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.answer: Escalate to CT or proceed to observation / diagnostic laparoscopy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: A non-visualised appendix does not exclude appendicitis. With persisting suspicion, further imaging (CT in a non-pregnant adult) or observation/diagnostic laparoscopy is indicated; discharge would be unsafe.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 24-year-old woman attends for a routine transabdominal pelvic ultrasound. The sonographer asks her to drink water and hold her urine beforehand. What is the primary reason a full bladder is required?
options: It compresses the ovaries to make them easier to measure
It provides an acoustic window and displaces bowel gas from the pelvis
It reduces patient movement during the scan
It increases blood flow to the uterus for Doppler assessment
It is needed to calculate an accurate post-void residual volume
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: It provides an acoustic window and displaces bowel gas from the pelvis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: A distended, fluid-filled bladder transmits ultrasound (acoustic window) and pushes gas-filled bowel out of the pelvis, allowing the pelvic organs to be visualised. Without it the scan is often non-diagnostic.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: Which of the following is a recognised limitation of transabdominal pelvic ultrasound compared with the transvaginal approach?
options: It cannot be used in children
It is invasive and poorly tolerated
It has lower resolution and is degraded by obesity and bowel gas
It cannot visualise large masses that extend out of the pelvis
It requires an empty bladder to work well
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: It has lower resolution and is degraded by obesity and bowel gas
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: TAUS is non-invasive and well tolerated and is actually better for large extra-pelvic masses, but its resolution is lower than transvaginal scanning and image quality is reduced by obesity, bowel gas and an empty bladder.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 27-year-old woman presents with acute right iliac fossa pain and a positive pregnancy test. A transabdominal ultrasound performed with a partially filled bladder appears unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure the patient that the scan excludes an ectopic pregnancy
Discharge with a routine outpatient follow-up scan in 6 weeks
Proceed to transvaginal ultrasound for higher-resolution assessment
Repeat the transabdominal scan in 24 hours only
Arrange a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: Proceed to transvaginal ultrasound for higher-resolution assessment
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: A technically limited or normal-appearing TAUS does not exclude an ectopic pregnancy. The correct step is to proceed to transvaginal ultrasound, which gives a higher-resolution close-up view of the adnexa and uterus.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 32-year-old woman with 6 weeks amenorrhoea and a positive pregnancy test is booked for transvaginal ultrasound. What bladder preparation should she be given?
options: Drink 1 litre of water and attend with a full bladder
Empty her bladder before the scan
Bladder state is irrelevant for transvaginal scanning
Take a diuretic one hour before
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: Empty her bladder before the scan
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: TVUS is performed with an empty bladder, the opposite of transabdominal scanning. A full bladder displaces the pelvic organs out of the high-frequency probe's near field and degrades the close-up image.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 58-year-old woman presents with postmenopausal bleeding. TVUS shows an endometrial thickness of 9 mm. What is the most appropriate next step?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. A stripe <4–5 mm is reassuring, but a thickened endometrium (here 9 mm) requires hysteroscopy and biopsy for histological diagnosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 29-year-old woman has a positive pregnancy test and serum hCG of 2200 IU/L. TVUS shows an empty uterus with a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. What does this most likely represent?
options: A normal very early intrauterine pregnancy
A completed miscarriage requiring no follow-up
Ectopic pregnancy / pregnancy of unknown location until proven otherwise
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: Ectopic pregnancy / pregnancy of unknown location until proven otherwise
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: With hCG above the discriminatory zone (~1500 IU/L) an intrauterine sac should be visible. An empty uterus with positive hCG is a pregnancy of unknown location and must be treated as ectopic until proven otherwise — gynae review and serial hCG. Free fluid heightens the concern.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 63-year-old woman presents with a single episode of postmenopausal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 9 mm. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge as the bleeding is due to atrophy
Start topical vaginal oestrogen and review
Refer on a 2-week-wait pathway for hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy
Arrange a transabdominal ultrasound for confirmation
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: Refer on a 2-week-wait pathway for hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: Postmenopausal bleeding with an endometrium >4 mm is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Tissue diagnosis is mandatory via urgent (2-week-wait) hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy; ultrasound alone cannot exclude carcinoma.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: Which transvaginal ultrasound appearance is most characteristic of adenomyosis rather than a fibroid?
options: A well-defined rounded hypoechoic mass with acoustic shadowing
A diffusely enlarged globular uterus with heterogeneous myometrium and a poorly defined junctional zone
A focal echogenic intracavity lesion with a feeding vessel
A bright shadowing linear echo in the central cavity
A single external fundal contour with an internal septum
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: A diffusely enlarged globular uterus with heterogeneous myometrium and a poorly defined junctional zone
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: Adenomyosis is diffuse: a globular uterus, heterogeneous myometrium (often with myometrial cysts) and an ill-defined/thickened junctional zone, with no discrete mass. The well-defined shadowing mass describes a fibroid; the intracavity lesion with a feeding vessel is a polyp; the bright shadowing linear echo is an IUCD; the internal septum describes a septate uterus.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: During which part of the menstrual cycle is the premenopausal endometrium typically thinnest on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: The endometrium is thinnest and brightest just after menses in the early proliferative phase, then progressively thickens to become maximal and most echogenic in the secretory (luteal) phase. This cyclical variation means there is no single normal thickness premenopausally.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 24-year-old woman has a 4 cm right adnexal cyst on transvaginal ultrasound: anechoic, thin-walled, no septations, with posterior acoustic enhancement. She is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure; this is a simple functional cyst — repeat ultrasound in 6–12 weeks
Commence the combined oral contraceptive pill to shrink the cyst
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: Reassure; this is a simple functional cyst — repeat ultrasound in 6–12 weeks
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: Anechoic, thin-walled cysts with posterior enhancement and no solid or septated components are simple functional cysts. In a young asymptomatic woman these are almost always benign and resolve; interval rescan confirms resolution. CA-125/RMI and oncology referral are for complex/suspicious masses.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 15-year-old presents with sudden severe left iliac fossa pain and vomiting. Ultrasound shows an enlarged oedematous left ovary with peripherally displaced follicles; colour Doppler demonstrates preserved arterial flow. What is the correct next step?
options: Reassure — preserved Doppler flow excludes torsion
Discharge with analgesia and outpatient follow-up
Start IV antibiotics for pelvic inflammatory disease
Request an outpatient MRI to characterise the mass
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: The clinical picture and enlarged oedematous ovary with peripheralised follicles indicate torsion. Because of dual blood supply, Doppler flow may persist — a normal Doppler does not exclude torsion. Torsion is an emergency; urgent laparoscopy to detorse can save the ovary.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 58-year-old post-menopausal woman has a complex right ovarian mass with solid areas, thick septations and moderate ascites. CA-125 is 480 U/mL. Which statement about her assessment is correct?
options: Polycystic ovarian morphology explains these findings
Her RMI is low because she is post-menopausal
The ground-glass echoes confirm a benign endometrioma
She has a high RMI and needs gynae-oncology MDT referral
The mass should simply be rescanned in 6 weeks
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: She has a high RMI and needs gynae-oncology MDT referral
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: RMI = U × M × CA-125. Post-menopausal status scores M = 3 (increasing, not lowering, the index), the ultrasound features (solid areas, multilocular, ascites) give a high U score, and CA-125 is markedly raised — yielding an RMI well above 200. This mandates referral to the gynae-oncology MDT.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 27-year-old woman is 6 weeks by dates with light bleeding. TVUS shows an empty uterus. Her serum hCG is 2100 IU/L. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Normal early intrauterine pregnancy, reassure and discharge
Complete miscarriage, no further action needed
hCG above the discriminatory zone with an empty uterus — ectopic must be actively excluded
Threatened miscarriage with a viable intrauterine pregnancy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: hCG above the discriminatory zone with an empty uterus — ectopic must be actively excluded
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: With serum hCG above ~1500 IU/L an intrauterine sac should be visible transvaginally. An empty uterus at this level is a pregnancy of unknown location that raises strong suspicion of ectopic; examine the adnexa and pouch of Douglas and consider serial hCG. It cannot be assumed normal, complete, or viable, and there are no molar features described.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: TVUS in a woman with a positive pregnancy test shows an intrauterine gestational sac with a mean sac diameter of 27 mm and no fetal pole. What does this indicate?
options: Viable intrauterine pregnancy, rescan not required
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: A mean gestational sac diameter ≥25 mm with no fetal pole (an empty sac) meets the criterion for a non-viable pregnancy. Because the sac is intrauterine and eccentric this is a miscarriage, not an ectopic pseudosac. A CRL ≥7 mm with no heartbeat is the other non-viable criterion; below these thresholds one would rescan in 7–14 days.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 31-year-old woman collapses at home. She has a positive pregnancy test, is tachycardic and hypotensive, reports right shoulder-tip pain, and has abdominal tenderness. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Arrange an outpatient TVUS before any intervention
Resuscitate and arrange urgent gynaecology review and theatre without delaying for imaging
Repeat serum hCG in 48 hours and review
Reassure and arrange EPAU follow-up in one week
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: Resuscitate and arrange urgent gynaecology review and theatre without delaying for imaging
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: This is a haemodynamically unstable ruptured ectopic — a life-threatening surgical emergency. Positive pregnancy test, shock, and shoulder-tip pain (diaphragmatic irritation from haemoperitoneum) demand immediate resuscitation with large-bore IV access, cross-match, and urgent gynaecology/theatre. Imaging, serial hCG, methotrexate, or outpatient follow-up would dangerously delay definitive surgical control of bleeding.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A bladder scanner measures a bladder as 8 cm (height) × 6 cm × 5 cm on three orthogonal diameters. Using the ellipsoid formula, which value best approximates the volume?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: Volume ≈ height × width × depth × 0.52 = 8 × 6 × 5 × 0.52 = 124.8... wait: 8×6×5 = 240, ×0.52 ≈ 125 mL. The correct product 240 cm³ × 0.52 ≈ 125 mL, so the intended answer is ~125 mL.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: An 80-year-old man voids and is scanned immediately, showing a post-void residual of 40 mL. How should this be interpreted?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: A PVR <50 mL indicates normal emptying. Up to ~100 mL may be acceptable in the elderly; 40 mL is reassuring and needs no intervention.
